title: Publication and voice
short: First printed in The Nation in 1912; title poem of Mew's first book (Poetry Bookshop, 1916; enlarged 1921). A farmer speaks in country dialect.
body: The poem made Mew's name when H. W. Massingham printed it in The Nation in 1912. Harold Monro's Poetry Bookshop issued The Farmer's Bride as a small book in 1916; the 1921 edition added eleven poems (published in America as Saturday Market). Thomas Hardy, who noticed the book in 1918 and befriended her, was foremost among her admirers. The poem is a dramatic monologue: the farmer tells his story without understanding all it reveals, a form Mew shared with Browning and Hardy. 'Three Summers since' places the marriage three years back, and 'chose' shows that the bride had little say.

title: Metre and rhyme
short: Four-beat lines with free rhyme and irregular indentation, lengthening to six-beat lines as feeling rises.
body: Mew's stanzas are irregular (9, 10, 10, 12 and 5 lines) and rhyme in couplets and cross-rhymes as the speaker's thought dictates. The base is a loose four-stress line close to speech. In stanza 4 the lines swell ('The short days shorten and the oaks are brown') into long, slow lines of landscape, before the final stanza's broken exclamations. Editors such as Warner and Copus note Mew's use of line length and indentation as a kind of score for the speaking voice.

title: 'bide and woo'
short: To linger and court. The farmer had no time for courtship at harvest: the marriage was a practical bargain.
body: 'Bide' (to wait, stay) is old and survives in dialect. The farmer's excuse, that there is more to do at harvest than courting, is offered as common sense, but it tells us the girl was married without being won. The admission 'Too young maybe' is the first sign of the speaker's half-conscious guilt. It also places the poem in the farming year that governs the whole story, from harvest to Christmas.

title: Dialect grammar
short: 'Us was wed', and later 'her be' and 'runned': West Country forms that give the farmer his own voice.
body: In south-western English dialects object pronouns often serve as subjects ('us was', 'her be'), and strong verbs can take regular endings ('runned'). The dialect recalls the Wessex voices of Hardy and William Barnes. The dialect is used sparingly, enough to mark the speaker as a countryman without parody. Readers should note that the dialect marks class and place, not stupidity: the farmer's landscape writing in stanza 4 is among the finest in the poem.

title: 'afraid of love'
short: The bride's terror is of sex, of the husband, and of human contact itself.
body: The line is the key to her character. Critics divide on emphasis: some read a portrait of sexual fear in a child-bride; feminist readers stress that she was married before she was ready and then imprisoned; others connect the poem with Mew's own fears and her sense of sexual difference, which Fitzgerald and Copus discuss biographically. The farmer reports the fear without understanding it.

anchor: Like the shut of a winter
title: 'the shut of a winter's day'
short: Her change is as sudden as the early dark of a winter afternoon; 'shut' means the close of day.
body: The 'shut' of the day, its shutting-in at evening, is an old expression recorded in the OED and in dialect. The simile ties the bride to the seasons, as the whole poem does: she withdraws as daylight fails, and stanza 4 is set in the shortening days before Christmas. 'Her smile went out' continues the image of a light put out.

title: fay
greek: Old French fae, from Latin fata, 'the Fates'
short: A fairy: the girl seems not quite human, like a creature of folklore.
body: 'Fay' is a literary and archaic word for a fairy. The farmer says she was not a woman but something from the other world. Folklore of changelings and fairy brides who cannot live among mortals lies behind the image, and it anticipates the animal similes (hare, mouse, leveret) that follow. The farmer reaches for fairy-tale language because he has no other words for what has happened to his marriage, and the word quietly removes his wife from the human world in which he could claim her.

title: 'runned'
short: Dialect past tense of 'run', placed at the climax of the stanza on its own indented line.
body: The regularised past tense ('runned' for 'ran') belongs to country speech. 'In the Fall' (autumn) is old English usage, now more common in America. Indenting the line sets the event apart: the turning point of the story is told in one short, flat line. The short, flat sentence after the long build-up of the stanza works almost like a news report, and the second stanza then tells the chase in vivid detail, as if the farmer were reliving it.

title: 'up-along across the down'
short: Uphill across the open downland; 'up-along' is West Country dialect.
body: 'Up-along' and 'down-along' are south-western expressions for going up or down the road or hill. The 'down' is open upland pasture (Old English dun, 'hill'), the landscape of Wessex. The word returns at the end in a different sense, 'the soft young down of her', so that the land she fled across and her body are joined in one word.

title: The hunted hare
short: The pursuit of the bride is described as a hunt, with the villagers and their lanterns as the hunters.
body: Hares are hunted and coursed; the image makes the men a hunting party and the bride their quarry. The farmer does not see the cruelty in his own comparison, and the dramatic irony is strong. The animal images (hare, mouse, leveret) consistently make her a wild creature, a view both affectionate and dehumanising. The lanterns place the chase at night, which makes the image of quarry and pursuers stronger still.

title: Church-Town
short: The village where the parish church stands; in Cornwall and the West Country 'churchtown' names such a settlement.
body: In Cornish and western usage a 'churchtown' is the hamlet round a parish church, which need not be the largest place in the parish. The chase runs across the farm's fields and the down to the church village. The capitals make it a proper name, typical of the speaker's local world. Reaching the village also means reaching the church where they were married, a quiet irony in the geography of the chase.

anchor: turned the key upon her, fast
title: Imprisonment
short: They lock her in: the farmer reports the captivity as a matter of course.
body: 'Fast' means securely. The rhyme last/fast closes the stanza like the door. Readers often compare the locked-up wife with the madwoman in the attic of Jane Eyre, and the final stanza places her 'up in the attic'. Mew's own family knew confinement: two of her siblings spent their lives in mental institutions, which Fitzgerald and Copus treat as background to her poems of shut-in women.

title: 'Not near, not near!'
short: Her eyes beg men to keep away; the only words of hers we hear are unspoken.
body: The bride never speaks in the poem: her plea is in her eyes, and the farmer says 'I've hardly heard her speak at all'. She is at ease with birds and rabbits but terrified of 'men-folk'. The phrase is set in quotation marks, as if her look had a voice, which shows how closely the farmer watches her. Her silence, and the farmer's fluent report of it, is the central asymmetry of the monologue.

title: Beasts at her call
short: The farm animals turn to her like children: she is at home with creatures as she is not with people.
body: The report, from 'the women', gives her a kind of power over animals, like a saint or a fairy woman. Some readers also hear a faint suggestion of the animals of the Nativity stable, which would prepare for the 'Christmas-time' of stanza 4, though this is an association rather than a certain allusion. The image also continues the contrast between her ease with creatures and her terror of men.

title: leveret
greek: Old French levrete, from Latin lepus, 'hare'
short: A young hare in its first year; the simile continues the hunted-hare image.
body: The OED defines a leveret as a hare in its first year. The stanza opens with a run of similes in praise (leveret, larch, violets) and then turns: 'To her wild self. But what to me?' Here the farmer's praise of her beauty changes into a sense of his own exclusion, the emotional turn of the poem. The young larch and the first wild violets keep the praise in the language of the countryside, the only vocabulary of beauty the farmer has.

title: The turn
short: The stanza's turning point: her beauty belongs to herself, not to him.
body: The two short sentences break the flowing similes. 'To her wild self' admits that she is complete in her own wildness; 'But what to me?' is the farmer's first open self-pity. Many readers find here the poem's balance of sympathy: we are moved both by her refusal and by his longing. A single rhyme (he/tree/she/me) binds the four lines together.

title: The winter landscape
short: Long, slow lines of late autumn: brown oaks, low smoke, a falling leaf, a magpie's feathers on the frost.
body: The lines lengthen to five and six beats, and the stanza becomes a still life of approaching winter that expresses the farmer's desolation without stating it. A magpie's scattered feathers on the black earth hint at a small death. The berries 'redden up to Christmas-time', and Christmas turns his thoughts to a household with 'some other' in it. The landscape becomes a language for feeling he cannot otherwise put into words.

title: rime
short: Hoarfrost: frozen dew whitening the ground.
body: The OED gives 'rime' as hoarfrost, from Old English hrim. The black earth spread white with frost echoes the black-and-white plumage of the magpie in the line above, a careful piece of colour design within the stanza. The whiteness of frost also continues the poem's movement into winter, and the contrast of black and white anticipates the closing contrast of the brown of her eyes and hair against the farmer's darkening mood.

title: The wish for a child
short: Christmas makes the farmer long for 'some other' in the house: the marriage is childless, apparently unconsummated.
body: The line is delicately indirect: 'some other' may mean a child, or simply company. Either way, the marriage has never become a family. The ungrammatical 'without there be' is dialect for 'unless there is'. The question, closed with an exclamation mark, is the farmer's most direct statement of loneliness before the confession of desire in the final stanza. Christmas, the feast of a child's birth, sharpens the sense of absence.

anchor: She sleeps up in the attic
title: The attic and the stair
short: She sleeps alone in the attic; only a stair lies between them, a short distance that cannot be crossed.
body: ''Tis but a stair / Betwixt us' measures the gap exactly: so near, so impossible. The archaic 'betwixt' belongs to the farmer's speech. The attic recalls Bertha Mason's confinement in Jane Eyre, and the line suggests both the farmer's restraint and the risk that he may not go on restraining himself; critics have read the ending as tender and as menacing.

anchor: her eyes, her hair, her hair!
title: The ending
short: The poem breaks into exclamations of desire: the 'down' of her skin, the brown of her eyes and hair.
body: 'Down' now means the fine soft hair of her skin, recalling the down they chased her across; 'brown' repeats her 'wide brown stare' and the brown oaks. The repetitions and broken syntax show desire overwhelming speech. Some readers feel sympathy for an inarticulate, frustrated man; others hear violence about to cross the stair. A reviewer of Copus's biography calls the poem 'a brilliant piece of imaginative ventriloquism' (London Grip), in which Mew voices a man's longing for a woman.
